newsitem.title: UK: European debt soars on German rate speculation.
newsitem.headline: European debt soars on German rate speculation.

text.p: European debt markets blasted to new highs on Friday, bolstered by renewed speculation of German interest rate cuts and a sparkling technical picture, traders and economists said.
The driving factor was talk that Germany might cut rates to help other ailing economies in Europe meet the criteria for a single currency, analysts said.
"All this rate cut speculation is coming back into the market," said Guido Hartenberger, a broker at Deutsche Bank in Frankfurt.
"People are thinking of the Bank of France, and a general round of rate cutting in Europe. People are even thinking the Bundesbank could be active before the year end," he said.
Markets have trudged higher all week but really took flight on Friday as German, French and British debt futures shot through to new highs.
December futures prices for German Bunds were quoted at 102.11 at 1304 GMT, up 47 basis points after piercing the psychological 102.00 level and hitting a new all-time high of 102.17.

December notionnel futures on the MATIF in Paris were trading 72 basis points up on the day at a new contract high of 129.00 while U.K. gilts touched a new contract high at 111-18 before trading back down to 111-13.
Itlaian BTPs, usually the most volatile of the pack, were showing a 50 basis point gain at 128.27, off the 128.70 all-time reached on Monday.

German cash markets were also breaking new ground with the 10-year bond yields breaching the 5-3/4 percent level, traders said. The 10-year Bund was quoted at 103.92, yielding 5.689 percent by midday in Europe.

Traders said the main impetus for the week's move higher was calls from Bank of France member Jean-Pierre Gerard for lower interest rates in both France and Germany to help jump-start the ailing French economy.
He said devalution of the French currency may be another option, echoing the views of other French currency watchers.
A trader at a U.S. bank in London said a report from SBC Warburg fanned the rate-cutting speculation.
"It seems to be gathering a little bit of pace," he said.
SBC Warburg said the Bundesbank would be pressured into cutting rates further as European countries struggled to meet the critieria for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
"With EMU still firmly on the agenda, the Bundesbank needs to provide more monetary stimulus to the rest of Europe. We expect Buba to fulfill its new obligations," it said.
Warburg forecast a 50 basis point cut in short-term German interest rates over the next three months.
But David Brickman, European economist at Yamaichi International here, said talk of interest rate cuts in Germany was being overplayed.
"The markets are very thin at the moment, so a small rumour travels a long way," he said."We're not expecting rate cuts. We're expecting steady rates in Germany."
Analysts said technical factors were also playing a major part in the market's move up.
Hartenburger said the BOBL future on the DTB exchange in Frankfurt outperformed Bunds this morning on a duration weighted basis. "That's a typical sign of rate-cut fervour coming back," he said.
The trader at the U.S. bank said the rest of the day's action may depend on the few U.S. traders who will be in after the Thanksgiving Day holiday on Thursday.
"U.S. players this afternoon are going to either take it up another half a point, or look at it, say there are no fundamental reasons for it, and sell it," he said.
